extracted.intended_audience: federal agency economists and regulatory analysts preparing regulatory impact analyses (RIAs) and OMB reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when and how agencies should identify, estimate, weight, and report distributional (differential) impacts of regulations within regulatory impact analyses, including questions of granularity, groups to analyze, use of distributional weights, and presentation of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider distributive impacts and equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider distributive impacts when deciding among alternatives and, as practicable and appropriate, recognize distributive impacts and equity in regulatory analysis (per Executive Orders 12866 and 14094).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Preamble and EOs direct agencies to consider distributional impacts; most commenters agreed distributional analyses are important and relevant for policymakers. Use distributional analysis where it informs regulatory choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary screening to target distributional analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should exercise discretion to perform preliminary screening of rules to determine which are most likely to have significant differentiated effects on particular demographic groups, and analyze important distributional effects in those cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB declined to mandate distributional analysis for all rules because not all rules of a given type will have important distributional effects and because distributional analysis can be complex and resource-intensive. Screening helps focus analytic resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not impose blanket requirement to use most granular data
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular A-4 should not advise agencies to always use the most granular information about benefits and costs as is feasible; no one-size-fits-all rule on granularity is advisable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While more granular data often improve accuracy, less granular data may sometimes be higher quality, more reliable, facilitate consistency across categories, or increase comparability with other analyses. Agencies should balance tradeoffs and consider whether units obscure distributional effects (e.g., summarizing by quartile can hide effects concentrated in the lowest decile).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose unit of analysis to avoid obscuring distributional effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing the unit of analysis, consider whether the unit could obscure the relevant distributional effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if a regulation affects only individuals in the lowest decile of income, summarizing by quartile will make the average size of such effects appear smaller. Consider granularity and unit choice relative to the distributional question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistency in group definitions where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent possible given available evidence, it is generally advisable for agencies to maintain consistency when identifying groups of interest across their regulations—particularly for regulations addressing similar concerns—or else explain their rationale for not doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circular A-4 applies across many agencies and contexts; requiring identical groups everywhere is inappropriate, but consistency aids comparability across rules when no rule-specific reason exists to differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: List possible groups to examine but do not mandate particular groups universally
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular A-4 will include a list of possible groups to examine (income, race/ethnicity, sex, gender, sexual orientation, disability, occupation, geography, firm size, industrial sector), but will not strictly call for the analysis of particular groups across all rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important distributional dimensions differ across regulations; the list is illustrative not exhaustive. Agencies should select groups relevant to the rule and data availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies may be required to produce distributional analysis when statute or EO demands it
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may have to produce distributional analyses when disaggregated analysis is required by the statute(s) under which the regulation is issued or called for by an Executive Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though OMB does not mandate distributional analysis generally, legal or executive directives can create obligations independent of Circular A-4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid requiring explanation for every omitted form of distributional analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring agencies to explain why they are not conducting each conceivable form of distributional analysis would be inadvisable and burdensome; OMB rejects a distinct requirement that would force numerous low-value explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies face limited resources; a special procedural requirement for distributional analyses could reduce flexibility to focus analytic attention where most valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for baseline cumulative exposures in health-related analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should emphasize distributional analysis of baseline cumulative exposure to health risks (e.g., pollution exposures) because differences in cumulative exposures and underlying health risk factors can cause regulation benefits to accrue unevenly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB highlighted this area as particularly useful for agencies to focus on when producing distributional analyses; commenters emphasized greater attention to baseline exposures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of distributional (income) weights is optional, not mandatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may choose to conduct benefit-cost analyses that apply weights to benefits and costs accruing to different groups to account for diminishing marginal utility of income, but OMB does not mandate such weighting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandating income weights would be inappropriate now because evidence/feasibility vary across cases. Weighed analyses can be primary or supplemental; agencies should decide based on informativeness and feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and transparency when applying distributional weights
rubrics_metrics.description: If you produce an estimate of net benefits utilizing such weights, the same weights should be applied to benefits and costs consistently in each analysis, and the weights used should be communicated clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should also present traditionally-weighted estimates (the usual equal-dollar-per-person aggregation) alongside any income-weighted estimates to allow comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat income-weighted estimates as primary if they are less informative
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should not treat estimates using weights that account for diminishing marginal utility as primary if they are less informative about the welfare effects of the regulation than traditionally-weighted estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB edited Circular A-4 to clarify this point to avoid agencies presenting less reliable weighted results as the main finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical implementation: constant-elasticity specification for weights
rubrics_metrics.description: One practical approach to implementing weights that account for diminishing marginal utility uses a constant-elasticity specification to determine the weights for subgroups defined by annual income.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circular A-4 suggests this specification and notes that population-average benefits/costs may be implicitly weighted already and analysts should strive to weight consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended elasticity of marginal utility (epsilon) for income-weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular A-4 provides an absolute value estimate of the income elasticity of marginal utility of 1.4 to use in income-weighted analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies can use this parameter (or justify alternatives) when implementing income-weighted benefit-cost calculations; the document discusses empirical/theoretical literature supporting weighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stratify population-average WTP by income when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: When the analyst has a population-average WTP (or WTA) and a good estimate of the elasticity of WTP with respect to income, the population-average measure should be stratified by income using the specified formula (WTP_i = WTP_bar * (y_bar_i / y_med)^eta) before income-weighting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After stratifying, use the absolute value of the income elasticity of marginal utility (epsilon) (e.g., 1.4) for income-weighted analysis. This allows combining stratified WTP across goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not apply income weights to VSL estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses should not apply income weights to values of mortality risk reductions (VSL) because population-average VSL values have already been implicitly weighted by income (the income elasticity of VSL approximates the absolute value of the income elasticity of marginal utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: VSL has long integrated income weighting; applying additional income weights would double-count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present both weighted and traditionally-weighted estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysts should present traditionally-weighted (equal-dollar) estimates alongside any income-weighted estimates; weighted estimates may be supplemental or primary depending on informativeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors practices for discounting and presentation of undiscounted annual streams: provide multiple presentations to enhance transparency and comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize feasibility limits and data constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should recognize the formidable conceptual and empirical challenges to identifying and estimating distributional effects (e.g., determining economic incidence, potential shifting of costs to workers/consumers), which can make distributional analysis infeasible in some circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB accepts that analytic methods and data availability will improve over time, but current resource and data limits justify agency discretion in many cases; where infeasible, agencies may rely on supplementary analyses as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended minimum disaggregations for some commenters (businesses and consumers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters recommended that guidance include instructions to analyze, at a minimum: 1) businesses being regulated when benefits are broad-based outside the regulated community; 2) businesses by size category, emphasizing smaller businesses; and 3) consumers of regulated products by income group, emphasizing lower quartile/quintile depending on data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB noted these recommendations but did not mandate them; agencies should consider such disaggregations when data allow and when relevant to the regulatory question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against cherry-picking by providing significance guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: To reduce the scope for agencies to 'cherry pick' when to conduct distributional analyses, commenters urged OMB to provide guidance on what rules are significant enough to require distributional analyses; OMB instead emphasized agency discretion with case-by-case assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB considered but did not adopt a mandatory category approach; agencies should use the preliminary screening process and document rationales for focusing analyses where most valuable.
